overview: The atlas calls this layer “Hispaniola (Spain)” from 1530 to 1715, but its geometry is not simply Hispaniola. In 1530 and 1600 one feature combines Jamaica, Puerto Rico, and Hispaniola. In 1650 and 1700 Jamaica disappears while Puerto Rico stays attached. Coastal cities fall outside the simplified shores. At 1715 eastern Hispaniola becomes “spain,” labeled Santo Domingo (Spain), western points become the anachronistic atlas id “haiti,” and San Juan receives an erroneous Danish Virgin Islands label. The map also lags politics. Spanish rule centered on Santo Domingo and named settlements, then contracted after forced depopulation in 1605 and 1606 opened space for western interlopers. French settlement expanded before the 1697 Treaty of Ryswick recognized France in the west; a precise border still did not appear at once. The layer therefore groups separate islands, simplifies shorelines, overstates uniform authority, and delays partition by eighteen years. This card treats it as an editorial aid. Its chapters use archives and excavated places to follow Taíno survival, African agency, slavery, government, family, childhood, work, food, health, water, waste, writing, faith, craft, trade, resistance, and continuity.

periods.title: 1530 to 1542: negotiated survival and sugar expansion
periods.summary: Enriquillo and other Taíno resisters forced a negotiated settlement in the early 1530s, while water-powered and animal-powered sugar works expanded. The agreement did not undo conquest, forced labor, or epidemic loss. It does prove that Indigenous people acted politically rather than simply disappearing from the story.

periods.title: 1542 to 1550: sugar wealth and incomplete conquest
periods.summary: Sugar production depended heavily on enslaved African labor, yet colonial authority remained incomplete. African and Indigenous maroons built communities, cultivated food, managed livestock, freed others, negotiated, and fought. Official population estimates are uncertain, but the evidence makes resistance central to the island's political history.

periods.title: 1550 to 1570: records name unequal lives
periods.summary: A 1555 to 1556 auction exposed the Atlantic slave trade's bodily violence. A 1558 prison list named free and enslaved, Black, Indigenous, mestizo, mulatto, male, and female detainees. Its phrase “El negro de gonçalo garçia çapatero con grillos” records a Black shoemaker in shackles, not his own voice.

periods.title: 1570 to 1586: ranches, contraband, destruction, and raid
periods.summary: Northern Puerto Real lived increasingly from cattle hides and illegal trade. Spanish officials forced its evacuation and destruction in 1579, but contraband persisted from nearby Bayahá. In 1586 Francis Drake captured and ransomed Santo Domingo, showing that the imperial capital's stone buildings did not guarantee security.

periods.title: 1586 to 1605: scarcity made smuggling ordinary
periods.summary: Licensed shipping dwindled while settlers sought foreign cloth, tools, food, and enslaved labor. Contraband became embedded across social groups. Sugar weakened as cattle, hides, and ginger gained importance. Crown officials answered economic disobedience with plans to empty the northern and western settlements.

periods.title: 1605 to 1620: the devastations remake the island
periods.summary: Authorities burned settlements and forcibly moved residents toward the southeast during the 1605 to 1606 devastations. Some people refused or escaped. Spanish patrols then concentrated inside a narrowed colony, while interlopers and self-sustaining communities occupied remote zones. Depopulation weakened the territorial claim it meant to defend.

periods.title: 1620 to 1655: western footholds and a defended capital
periods.summary: French, Dutch, and English interlopers traded and planted tobacco in western Hispaniola after forced depopulation opened space. In 1655 an English expedition attacked Santo Domingo but failed against its defenders, then seized Jamaica. The event protected the capital without restoring uniform Spanish control over the island.

periods.title: 1655 to 1670: two colonial projects take shape
periods.summary: French settlement expanded from Tortuga and the western coast while Spanish administration remained centered in Santo Domingo. France's West India Company signaled formal colonial intent in 1664. People in farms, ranches, ports, maroon settlements, and garrisons experienced overlapping claims rather than a clean border drawn overnight.

periods.title: 1670 to 1697: rivalry precedes diplomatic partition
periods.summary: French and Spanish settlers fought intermittently as France expanded in the west and Spain lacked resources to garrison the whole island. The 1697 Treaty of Ryswick recognized French possession in the western part. It did not immediately survey a precise boundary or erase cross-border movement.

periods.title: 1697 to 1715: continuity after Ryswick
periods.summary: Spanish Santo Domingo continued in the east and French Saint-Domingue grew in the west after Ryswick, while the boundary remained unsettled. The atlas waits until 1715 to replace its island-wide Spanish id. That eighteen-year delay is a map seam, not the date when two societies suddenly appeared.

sections.title: Read the atlas shape before treating it as history

items.text: The index contains one generated record named “Hispaniola (Spain),” dated approximately 1530 to 1715. It is absent from the 1500 map and has a modern-island imported summary, but no card or researched override. Those database facts do not establish that every resident, port, mountain settlement, or neighboring island shared one Spanish identity or government.

In 1530 and 1600 the target is a three-component MultiPolygon. Its decoded pieces cover coarse versions of Jamaica, Puerto Rico, and Hispaniola. Santiago, Higüey, Hinche, Cap-Haïtien, Port-au-Prince, Léogâne, and San Juan fall inside, although several coastal city coordinates miss the simplified shore. This is an imperial grouping, not one island outline.

The 1650 and 1700 versions drop the Jamaica component but retain Puerto Rico and Hispaniola as one label. Both use the same two-component decoded geometry. A reader therefore cannot interpret a color change as a surveyed border, a demographic census, or evidence that control was equally strong across hundreds of kilometers.

Santo Domingo, Puerto Plata, Azua, Les Cayes, Tortuga, Saona, and Gonâve all fall outside the target under this atlas point test, despite their relevance to the history being told. Coarse shorelines can miss real coastal places. The card uses named evidence rather than making the polygon decide who existed.

At 1715 the exact id disappears. Sampled eastern points become “spain,” labeled Santo Domingo (Spain); western points become the anachronistic atlas id “haiti”; and San Juan becomes the unrelated “virgin-islands-danemark.” Ryswick had recognized France in the west in 1697. The lag and Puerto Rico error reveal an editorial seam, not new states appearing together.

sections.title: See colonial government, courts, cities, and their limits

items.text: Santo Domingo concentrated a governor, cabildo or town council, Real Audiencia, chancery, customs house, cathedral, monasteries, and other institutions. These offices made the city a major center of Spanish imperial administration. Their surviving masonry demonstrates organized power, but an impressive courthouse could issue orders much farther than officials could reliably enforce them.

The city's plaza-centered grid, rebuilt on the west bank of the Ozama after 1502, influenced later Spanish American town planning. Straight streets organized government, worship, commerce, and elite property. They did not make the colony socially tidy: enslaved workers, servants, craftspeople, traders, children, migrants, and prisoners filled the planned blocks with unequal lives.

A 1545 royal letter discussed about one hundred enslaved and free residents of Moorish or Berber background, including skilled masons and carpenters who were married and had children. The episode shows imperial sorting by religion, ancestry, status, and usefulness, while residents and city officials argued for locally valuable families to remain.

Contraband spread because official fleets and legal imports did not meet local needs. Residents traded with foreign Protestant merchants despite royal bans, linking survival to disobedience. The practice crossed social levels, so “Spanish colony” describes a jurisdictional claim without proving that every transaction followed Spain's commercial rules or every inhabitant shared imperial loyalties.

Drake's force captured Santo Domingo in 1586, looted it, and demanded ransom. A Spanish royal letter treated the attack as part of the Anglo-Spanish conflict and ordered a response. The raid damaged a symbolic capital, but the colony continued. Stone walls, titles, and paperwork were real achievements without being invulnerability spells.

sections.title: Keep Taíno people, survival, and agency in the story

items.text: Spanish conquest, forced gold labor, food seizure, violence, and introduced disease caused catastrophic Taíno death. The scale is debated, and older claims of complete extinction erase survivors. Indigenous people joined new households, moved, resisted, and transmitted knowledge. A demographic disaster can be both devastating and followed by living continuity.

Surviving Indigenous communities maintained traditions in agriculture, pottery, weaving, food, music, and healing. These practices changed as people navigated coercion and new African and European neighbors. Continuity does not mean an untouched pre-1492 world; it means people carried skills, words, memories, kinship, and choices through colonial disruption.

Enriquillo's long resistance forced negotiation in the early 1530s and secured an autonomous Indigenous settlement. Other Taíno people escaped, fought, or built rural communities. Calling the settlement a simple Spanish gift reverses the evidence: it emerged because Indigenous organizing made conquest expensive and incomplete.

At El Cabo in eastern Hispaniola, archaeology follows a Taíno household landscape occupied for centuries into the first decades of European contact. House remains and objects make domestic life visible without supplying every person's name. One excavated community can challenge disappearance stories, but it cannot stand for the entire island after 1530.

A 1558 Santo Domingo prison inventory lists Antonio as “yndio,” while a 1549 report described Indigenous maroons operating with a Black leader near La Vega. Both records come through colonial officials and coercive institutions. Even so, they directly refute the idea that Indigenous presence or political action had ended before this card begins.

sections.title: Follow African lives through slavery, freedom, and resistance

items.text: Early sugar investment joined machinery, skilled technicians, and coerced labor. A 1518 license authorized technicians plus fifteen enslaved Black men and two enslaved Black women for a mill. The document records a business plan from above; it does not tell us the workers' names, consent, families, knowledge, or strategies for surviving the work.

By the mid-sixteenth century, Africans outnumbered Spaniards in some estimates and powered sugar, ranching, transport, construction, domestic service, and craft. Maroons created settlements, grew varied crops, managed feral livestock, freed people from slavery, and defended territory. Those communities made Spanish conquest partial rather than completed.

A confiscated Portuguese ship led to a 1555 to 1556 Santo Domingo auction of enslaved people. Records describe women, men, and a small girl through color, illness, branding, price, and purchaser. The detail is evidence of commodification and bodily harm, never permission to treat the people themselves as collectible curiosities.

Catalina Fernández, a free Black woman, obtained permission to sail from Seville to Santo Domingo in 1539 with her daughter Francisca de Castilla. Their license shows voluntary Black migration and a family moving together across the Atlantic. It also shows how freedom still required documents that officials could demand and inspect.

María de Cota was born in Santo Domingo, enslaved in a household that moved to Seville, manumitted through a will, and later traveled with her young daughter. Her record preserves mobility, motherhood, legal strategy, and attachment to birthplace. It cannot tell us whether every hoped-for opportunity became real.

sections.title: Meet families, children, learners, and unequal classrooms

items.text: Just before this layer begins, a 1527 crown order sought more enslaved Black women and promoted marriage among Black residents because officials feared rebellion by a male-majority population. That was population management, not family welfare. People still formed relationships and pursued kin under conditions that let owners and officials buy, sell, move, or separate them.

The 1545 correspondence about Moorish and Berber residents described men and women, marriages, children, masons, carpenters, enslavement, and freedom in the same dispute. Family life crossed legal categories, while authorities judged households by ancestry, religion, labor, and supposed danger. The archive reveals families, but mostly when government wanted to classify them.

Puerto Real archaeology places non-European servants and possible family members inside households; less privileged European residents might have an Indigenous wife or mother. These observations make mixed households visible while warning us how badly elite inventories and masonry excavations undercount laborers, informal kin, and families living in humbler buildings.

Santo Domingo housed an early university, while book hardware appears in better-off excavated Puerto Real households. Together they show organized higher study and some household literacy. Neither source provides an enrollment list or proves broad access, so the card cannot say which children, women, workers, or rural families studied there.

Excavated Puerto Real homes yielded gaming pieces, children's toys, a jaw harp, needlework evidence, and book hardware. These finds place play, sound, handiwork, and reading beside labor. Fun fact: someone could finish chores, lose a game piece, and make music without leaving a diary about any of it.

sections.title: Enter homes, kitchens, wardrobes, and working days

items.text: Puerto Real's better-off households used walled compounds, several rooms, tiled floors, patios, drains, imported ceramics, glass, wood furniture, and horses. Archaeologists also expect many humbler wood-and-thatch buildings that left fainter traces. A masonry house is easier to find centuries later, which can make wealth look more normal than it was.

Cooking in Spanish households often used Indigenous- or African-made pottery. Cooks combined manioc, turkey, turtle, and local resources with Iberian preferences for mammal meat. The result was neither purely Spanish nor a timeless “island diet.” Enslaved and Indigenous expertise shaped what appeared on colonial tables, although owners often claimed the household's prestige.

Sugar complexes joined cane fields, animal or hydraulic mills, boiling and purging spaces, warehouses, roads, rivers, forest fuel, technical knowledge, and forced labor. Their surviving machinery is an engineering achievement and a landscape of exploitation at once. Admiring how gears and water moved must include asking whose bodies kept the system moving.

As sugar weakened, ranching, hides, and ginger grew more important. Enslaved workers herded cattle, processed hides, farmed, transported goods, and maintained estates, while maroons also managed livestock outside Spanish control. “Cowboy” is too cheerful a shortcut here: similar skills operated under radically different conditions of bondage, freedom, and flight.

A Nuremberg thimble, imported goods, locally made pottery, and a 1558 list naming a Black shoemaker show craft work without reconstructing one universal outfit. Clothes could display rank, but making or repairing them did not guarantee freedom, wealth, or comfort. One thimble also cannot tell us who held it.

sections.title: Move sugar, hides, ceramics, people, and contraband

items.text: Spain's licensed trade system routed legal commerce through approved ships and officials, but fewer vessels called as richer mainland colonies drew attention away. Settlers sought alternatives. Smuggling supplied manufactured goods and enslaved people while joining Catholic residents to Dutch, English, French, and Portuguese traders whom imperial law called enemies or intruders.

Puerto Real exported cattle hides through illegal rescate with foreign ships. The crown ordered the town abandoned and destroyed in 1579, yet residents continued trading from Bayahá until authorities destroyed that settlement in 1605. Burning a marketplace could move commerce and families; it did not burn away demand, skill, or maritime routes.

On the eve of this atlas layer, officials worried that settlers left for places where they could exploit larger Indigenous workforces. Wealthy colonists proposed tax-free imports of equipment and enslaved Africans instead. The 1528 plan treated coerced labor as a remedy for depopulation, exposing how “development” tied investment, settlement, and bondage together.

A royal license from 1518 allowed four enslaved Black Christians to travel with a Santo Domingo notary. That year, treasury officers also requested broader access to enslaved labor. Legal paperwork connected the colony to the coercive Atlantic system. A stamped permit changed an importer's legal risk, not the enslaved person's lack of consent.

Puerto Real households used pottery and glass from Spain and Italy, later joined by German stoneware, Chinese goods, and items linked to French, English, or Portuguese trade. Objects crossed political borders more easily than atlas colors suggest. Archaeology identifies connections, but a shard cannot by itself reveal whether it arrived by gift, purchase, theft, or contraband.

sections.title: Treat illness, survive epidemics, and preserve healing knowledge

items.text: A late-seventeenth-century archival memory credited an unnamed Black woman with sheltering and treating sick people in her bohío around 1497 to 1501, before the formal San Nicolás hospital. The memory does not securely establish her legal status or methods. It does preserve a Black caregiver at the origin of colonial institutional medicine.

Santo Domingo's San Nicolás de Bari became an early formal hospital, alongside the cathedral, customs house, university, and court. “Hospital” did not mean a modern emergency department with antibiotics. It joined shelter, nursing, food, worship, administration, and unequal access in a society where labor status and ancestry shaped treatment.

Taíno survivors maintained healing traditions as well as agriculture, weaving, pottery, food, and music. African and European knowledge also entered households and institutions. The record supports medical exchange, but it rarely lets us assign every remedy to one origin or decide whether a particular patient trusted a healer, friar, midwife, relative, or several.

Introduced diseases helped drive catastrophic Indigenous mortality, and a 1586 smallpox epidemic also reduced the enslaved population. Hunger, overwork, violence, displacement, and poor shelter could magnify illness. Exact totals remain debated, so the safest lesson is causal and human: epidemics struck societies already made more vulnerable by colonial coercion.

The 1555 to 1556 auction described a small enslaved girl with visible skin disease and a brand before a tailor bought her. The record documents inspection for sale, not a diagnosis or care plan. Her illness should direct attention to bodily harm, childhood vulnerability, and the archive's cold commercial gaze.

sections.title: Ask where water, drains, waste, and toilets actually went

items.text: Archaeology in Santo Domingo has identified a sixteenth-century system carrying water from a noria near San Francisco toward the main plaza, plus springs, household wells, and small lifting devices. Some household norias were operated by enslaved people. Urban water engineering therefore joined public infrastructure to coerced daily labor.

Santo Domingo's sixteenth-century conduit moved lifted water toward the main plaza, while household wells and smaller norias served other users. This was infrastructure, but it was not a universal tap network or sewer. A pipe beneath a street can be impressive without secretly becoming modern indoor plumbing for every home.

No water wells have been located in the excavated Puerto Real areas described by the Florida Museum. That absence does not prove residents lacked wells or safe water; unexcavated zones, rivers, containers, rain collection, and perishable equipment remain possibilities. “Not found” is an archaeological result, not permission to invent a convenient answer.

Sugar mills stood near rivers and forests because production needed water, transport, and large amounts of fuel wood. Industrial water use therefore affected where people worked and how landscapes changed. The channels served machinery first; they should not be mistaken for equal household access to clean drinking water or effortless washing.

The published Puerto Real synthesis identifies drains, patios, boundaries, corrals, and gardens but no securely interpreted privy or toilet. People obviously produced waste; the fixture and disposal route are the missing evidence. Fun fact withheld by archaeology: no excavated sign says “colonial bathroom, please form an orderly line.”

sections.title: Hear language, faith, creativity, and the 1715 continuation

items.text: Written-language sample from a 1558 Spanish prison list: “El negro de gonçalo garçia çapatero con grillos.” CUNY DSI supplies the translation, “Gonçalo Garçia, Black, shoemaker, with shackles.” This is a clerk's terse administrative Spanish, with period spelling and an ambiguous “de”; it records confinement and work, not the prisoner's own voice.

That Spanish sentence cannot stand for Taíno languages or the many African languages carried to Hispaniola. Colonial clerks favored the language of government and often compressed people into racial and legal labels. Taíno words and knowledge survived in Caribbean speech and practice even where alphabetic records failed to preserve full Indigenous voices.

Santo Domingo's cathedral, monasteries, hospital, university, customs house, fortress, and grid influenced later cities. These are architectural and institutional achievements, built through Indigenous, African, and European skill within conquest and slavery. Naming coercion does not erase craft; admiring craft does not absolve the system that commanded and benefited from it.

At Puerto Real, locally made pottery, cooking, medicine, music, dance, religion, art, architecture, and language show Afro-Indigenous-European cultural formation. Archaeologists stress women's central role in domestic exchange. “Mixture” must not sound frictionless: creativity happened amid unequal power, forced migration, survival, intimacy, resistance, and ordinary family decisions.

The atlas ends this id in 1715, eighteen years after Ryswick recognized a French western possession. Eastern Spanish Santo Domingo, western Saint-Domingue, Taíno descendants, African communities, mixed families, towns, farms, churches, maroons, and trade all continued. The endpoint corrects a belated map label; it does not describe a people's extinction or a colony vanishing.

ending.text: At the 1715 atlas seam, “hispaniola-spain” disappears. Sampled eastern points move to “spain,” labeled Santo Domingo (Spain), and western points move to the anachronistic atlas id “haiti”; Puerto Rico is misassigned to a Danish Virgin Islands layer. Ryswick had recognized French possession in the west in 1697, while no precise border was fixed then. People, families, farms, maroon communities, institutions, and trade continued on both sides. This is a delayed, flawed relabeling, not a fall or extinction.
